summary: Help 9-10 year-olds shift from term-to-term (recursive) reasoning to position-to-term (functional) rules so they can jump straight to any term, and build a reusable percentage toolkit from 10% and 5%. The core move is forcing the 'jump' — asking for a far term (20th, 100th) so listing becomes impractical and a general rule is needed — then insisting the rule be verified against a known term. Equivalent calculation methods (×25 = ×100 then ÷4) should be justified by why they work, not memorised as tricks.
misconceptions: Predicts the 20th term by extending term-by-term (or drawing all terms) instead of a position-to-term rule
Uses only a term-to-term rule ('add 4') and cannot jump to a far term efficiently
Treats each percentage as a separate conversion rather than building from 10% and 5%
States a general rule from a few cases without verifying it on a known term

activities.title: Sequence machine: force the jump to a far term
steps: Look at a sequence such as 5, 9, 13, 17, … and notice the constant difference of 4.
Try to reach the 20th term by extending term-by-term and feel how slow and error-prone this gets.
Make a table pairing position (n) with term so the relationship becomes visible.
State a position-to-term rule (e.g. term = 4×position + 1) and use it to jump straight to the 20th term (81).
Check the rule against a known early term (does it give the 3rd term correctly?) before trusting it.
Then be asked for the 100th term, where listing is clearly impractical, so the general rule proves its worth.
activities.insight: A position-to-term rule lets you reach any term in one step, which counting-on cannot do efficiently; a rule is only trustworthy once checked against a known term.

activities.title: Build a percentage toolkit from 10% and 5%
steps: Find 10% of an amount by dividing by 10.
Find 5% by halving the 10% value.
Assemble 35% of an amount by combining three 10% parts and one 5% part (e.g. 35% of £80 = 24 + 4 = 28).
Explain that this is a general method: name which parts you'd combine to make a different percentage such as 65%.
Use a percentage bar or double number line (100% → 10% → 5% → 35%) to see how the parts make up the whole.
Use a ratio table to scale the 10% and 5% parts to a different total amount, showing the method generalises across amounts, not just one figure.
activities.insight: Any multiple of 5% can be built by combining derived facts (10% and 5%) rather than treated as a separate one-off conversion. Other percentages, such as 37%, need further derived facts like 1%. This gives a reusable method that scales to any amount.

activities.title: Justify an equivalent calculation method
steps: Work out why multiplying any number by 25 can be done by multiplying by 100 then dividing by 4.
Use a factor/equivalent-fraction model (25 = 100 ÷ 4) to explain the equivalence, not just assert it.
Try the method on a worked example and check the result matches the direct multiplication.
Explain in words why the two routes must give the same answer.
activities.insight: Equivalent methods and shortcuts are reliable because of structure (25 = 100 ÷ 4), not because they are isolated tricks; understanding why lets you judge when a shortcut applies.

activities.title: Probe and discuss the generality of a rule
steps: Answer 'how would you find the 100th term — does your method still work?' to test whether a rule is genuinely general.
Evaluate a classmate's claim: 'the 20th term is 4×(the 5th term) — is that right? check it on the 2nd term' and explain the flaw.
Explain how to build 35% of £80 from 10% and 5%, and whether the same method gives 65%.
Explain why ×25 equals ×100 then ÷4.
activities.insight: Stating a rule is not enough; its generality must be tested against far cases and known terms, and proportional shortcuts that wrongly scale the constant offset along with the term fail these checks.

checkQuestion: A sequence starts 5, 9, 13, 17, … What is the 20th term? Don't write out all twenty — tell me the general rule you'd use and how you found it.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a position-to-term rule (term = 4×position + 1, so the 20th is 81) reached by linking the constant difference 4 to the position, and a check against a known term. Using the rule to jump, not counting on, is the target.
